title: Jesus walked into the water…
paragraphs:
Jesus walked into the water…
not because He was guilty—
but because He was willing.
And that changes everything.

Because if you misunderstand this moment,
you will misunderstand the heart of the Gospel.

John the Baptist was baptizing people who were confessing sin.
Broken people. Guilty people. Repentant people.
Then suddenly—Jesus appears.

No record of sin.
No confession to make.
No stain to wash away.
And yet… He steps forward.

John is shaken.
“I need to be baptized by You, and do You come to me?” (Matthew 3:14)

In other words:
“This is backwards.”
And it was.
Because the Kingdom of God often looks like reversal.

The Holy One standing in a sinner’s place.
The Clean One stepping into dirty water.
The Righteous One entering a moment meant for the unrighteous.
But Jesus responds with something profound:
“Let it be so now; it is proper for us to do this to fulfill all righteousness.” (Matthew 3:15)
That phrase—“fulfill all righteousness”—is the key.

Jesus wasn’t repenting.
He was aligning Himself fully with the Father’s will.
He was beginning His mission… the right way.

Not by distancing Himself from sinners—
but by identifying with them.
Let that sink in.

Before He preached to sinners…
He stood with them.

Before He died for sinners…
He stepped into their place.

Before He carried the cross…
He entered the water.

This was not symbolic weakness.
This was intentional humility.
And humility is always the doorway to divine assignment.
But there’s something even deeper happening here.
This moment is a preview.
A foreshadowing.
A living prophecy.

Because the water represents what He would ultimately step into—
our sin, our shame, our judgment.
He didn’t just observe humanity’s condition.
He entered it.
Fully.
Willingly.
Without resistance.
The baptism was a shadow of the cross.

He went under the water…
just like He would go into death.

He came out of the water…
just like He would rise again.
This wasn’t just obedience.
This was declaration:
“I am the One who will take their place.”
And heaven could not stay silent.
The Spirit descended like a dove.
The Father’s voice broke through the sky:
“This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” (Matthew 3:17)
Did you notice when that happened?

Not after miracles.
Not after sermons.
Not after the cross.
Before anything.

Before Jesus proved anything publicly…
He was already fully approved.
That means His identity was not built on performance.
It was rooted in relationship.
And here’s the part many people miss:
Because of Christ, that same pattern applies to you.

You don’t fight for God’s approval.
You fight from it.

You don’t earn sonship.
You receive it.

You don’t perform to be loved.
You live because you already are.
But don’t overlook this:
Jesus stepping into the water was also a call.
A model.
An invitation.
Because later, He would tell His followers to be baptized too.

Not because water saves—
but because obedience reveals surrender.
Baptism becomes our response to what He already did.
He identified with us in His baptism…
So now we identify with Him in ours.
Let’s bring it closer.
Some of you are waiting until you feel “clean enough” before stepping toward God.
That moment will never come.
Jesus didn’t wait for a perfect environment.
He stepped into imperfect water.
And if the sinless Son of God was willing to stand in a place meant for sinners…
What makes us think we need to fix ourselves before coming to Him?
You don’t get clean, then come to Jesus.

You come to Jesus…
and He makes you clean.
Let these truths stay with you:

• Jesus didn’t need baptism—but baptism needed Him.
• He stepped into our place long before we ever stepped toward His.
• The water didn’t cleanse Him—He came to cleanse us.
• Identity comes before assignment.
• God’s approval is received, not achieved.
So the next time you picture that moment in the Jordan…
Don’t just see water.
See love.
See humility.
See a Savior who refused to stay distant.

See a King who walked into your condition…
so you could walk into His righteousness.

Engagement Question:
What speaks to you more about Jesus—His power to save, or His willingness to step into your place before saving you?
